title: Laser Weapons Are Finally Headed to the Battlefield: The US Military Has Already Spent $15 Billion on R&D
dek: Lasers are the sniper rifles of directed energy weapons; microwaves are the electronic shotguns. The US military is shifting from R&D to procurement, but what's really scarce is cheap interceptors — whether you can win every engagement yet still not afford to fight is the key question.
why: This episode lays out the real bottlenecks of laser weapons from physics and combat economics, and also covers supply chains and the defense procurement landscape — suited to anyone following defense tech and defense stocks.
who: Defense industry analysts, defense tech VCs, readers tracking China's military modernization, and anyone trying to understand the US military's munitions-consumption anxiety.
skip: The first few minutes of event announcements and small talk — skip straight to 05:08, where the guest's military background begins.

points.h: A laser is a sniper rifle, a microwave is a shotgun
points.body: Wayne uses ‘a laser is a sniper rifle, a microwave is an electronic shotgun’ to distinguish the two kinds of directed energy weapons: a laser concentrates energy into a narrow beam, attacking one target at a time and burning through with thermal energy; a microwave's beam is wider and can affect the electronic systems of multiple targets at once. GAO says high-power microwave peak power can reach 100 megawatts, but comparing that directly with the kilowatts of a continuous-wave laser is meaningless, because the two have completely different characteristics: lasers try to raise power, microwaves try to amplify area effects. Which you pick depends on the target — drone swarms suit microwaves, a single ballistic missile can only be handled by a laser. The reason is that microwaves can make drones fail and crash, but they can't destroy a single missile flying at high speed the way a laser can.

points.h: Chemical lasers failed on volume and logistics
points.body: After the laser was invented in the 1960s, the military immediately saw its potential, but the real problems were power and volume. In the 1990s the US-Israeli Tactical High Energy Laser and DARPA's MIRACLE chemical laser both successfully shot down rockets, but the entire system was enormous and logistically complex, and the program was terminated in 2006. Chemical lasers get light energy directly from a chemical reaction and don't need electricity — the oxygen-iodine laser, for example, was mounted on a Boeing 747 (YAL-1) in an attempt to fly near a ballistic missile launch area and intercept, but carrying chemicals on an aircraft was simply too dangerous. Today the core metric of technological progress is called SWaP: size, weight and power. Lasers used to be as big as a building, precisely because generating beam energy required enormous amounts of electrical power, and today's goal is to fit them into trucks and warships.

points.h: The handheld laser bottleneck is power compression
points.body: Asked why the handheld laser guns from sci-fi movies still don't exist, Wayne points to the bottleneck as ‘generating and compressing power’. The fastest land platform today is the high-energy laser mounted on a Stryker armored vehicle, at 50 kilowatts, drawing on the vehicle's own power generation; if you want a 5-kilowatt beam to shoot down drones, you may need 15 to 25 kilowatts of input power, and without enough power supply you can only watch the drone fly at you with no way to respond. Electricity is the core constraint, not a gap in optical technology. This also explains why, after decades of development, laser weapons are only now approaching the turning point of large-scale deployment.

points.h: You still have to keep the expensive missiles
points.body: Many people assume lasers can replace interceptor missiles costing millions of dollars each, but Wayne warns that if the other side launches a hypersonic weapon, you won't want to gamble on a laser hitting a Mach 5 target exactly. So the real framework is ‘integrated air and missile defense’ — a combination of layered defenses. The cost advantage of lasers and microwaves is a low cost per shot, but you have to wait for the target to come within kill range; against a weapon traveling at 4,000 miles per hour, you still need carefully engineered interceptors like PAC-3 and SM-3. Israel is the best example: Arrow 2/3 intercepts long-range ballistic missiles, David's Sling blocks medium-range, Iron Dome blocks rockets, and now Iron Beam is added to take down drones.

points.h: Battlefield commanders don't care about unit price
points.body: On who thinks about cost when firing, Wayne divides decisions into four levels: tactical, operational, strategic and national. A platoon leader or company commander at the front, facing a threat, will use every necessary means to protect the force and doesn't care at all how much a missile costs; but at the theater commander and Pentagon level, you have to consider whether it's worth using a $4.1 million PAC-3 to take down a $30,000 drone. So the demand for ‘cheap weapons’ comes from the top, not the bottom. Only national-level decision-makers factor munitions consumption and supply chain problems into their choices. That distinction explains why, after being worn down in Yemen and the Red Sea, the US military began tilting toward low-cost interception options.

points.h: The US military is shifting to low-cost munitions
points.body: Over the past few decades, the US military stockpiled more and more expensive precision interceptors for high-end peer warfare, and then in Yemen and the Red Sea it was worn down by the other side's drones to the point where it had to change. Wayne says the Pentagon is signing multi-year framework agreements to sharply increase production, but the core is the realization that you can't forever answer cheap threats with expensive solutions. One of his core judgments: in a future conflict, ‘you can win every engagement and still lose the war economically’. This is exactly the market demand for low-cost interception systems like Coyote, Vampire and APKWS. Battlefield commanders need more options in hand, rather than only being able to fire off expensive missiles.

points.h: Startups are cutting into the middle market
points.body: Asked whether laser weapons will be strangled by the defense giants because of the innovator's dilemma, Wayne argues the giants will indeed continue to dominate the high-end interceptor market, but the low-end and middle solutions have already gone to five companies holding DoD contracts: Coaspire, Leidos, Anduril, Zone 5 and Castilian. What the Pentagon wants is a scale of tens of thousands, not an increment from 620 to 2,000. So in the short term the giants have the advantage, and within three to five years upstarts like Anduril may seize the middle market. That also means that when investing in defense stocks you can't just stare at the traditional giants — you have to see who benefits from the procurement shift.

points.h: AI killer robots are still a long way off
points.body: Wayne says that inside the Pentagon, AI is currently used only for intelligence analysis, tagging imagery for analysts and spotting changes, not for making strike decisions. His earlier research at the war college centered on ‘AI and levels of trust’. From target identification to tactical strike it is still entirely ‘human-in-the-loop’ — AI can help you find a target and raise an alert, but the final decision is still made by human commanders and intelligence analysts. Some worry AI will decide on its own to destroy a target; Wayne says that future is still a long way off. The risk models aren't ready, so the Pentagon currently does not use AI for autonomous killing, but rather to replace tedious work in military intelligence screening.
